title: What is known about 1RB0RD_0LC0LF_1RD1LB_0RE---_1RA0LC_0LA1LF
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0RD_0LC0LF_1RD1LB_0RE---_1RA0LC_0LA1LF.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. The head sweeps between the ends over a background of 100 blocks, and the tape grows by 3 cells every few sweeps. A handful of short defects ride on the background, change phase each sweep and drift left at different speeds. Lean proves the shift rules over the background and the two halting patterns; the run has not halted in 1010 steps, but the defects' interactions are not decoded.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (D1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: Shift rules, for every length
claims.text: Going right: A turns (100)^n into (001)^n and (1010)^n into (0101)^n; D turns (001)^n into (010)^n and (0101)^n into (1010)^n; E turns (0101)^n into (1010)^n; each for every n and every tape around.

claims.title: The two ways to halt
claims.text: The only halt is D reading a 1, and D is entered only from A1 = 0RD and C0 = 1RD. So A reading 1 1, or C reading 0 1, halts at once, whatever the tape around.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 67,084 cells have been visited and 22,367 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: exp/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.054). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.483).

claims.title: No halt in 10<sup>10</sup> steps
claims.text: tools/c/tmrun.c: 1010 steps from blank tape without a halt (69,643 ones). In 109 steps D was entered about 12.5 million times and always read a 0.

claims.title: No halt in the first 2.72×10<sup>19</sup> steps (exact macro run)
claims.text: A macro simulator (blocks of 6 cells, long runs of equal blocks crossed in one go; exact: every macro step is a run of the machine, counted step for step) ran from blank tape to step 27,236,709,152,426,296,878 without a halt. At this block size it gives the same state, head position and tape as the direct simulator after 2,000,001,031 steps. This is a bounded run and says nothing about later steps.

claims.title: No closed tape language from windows up to 7
claims.text: bbtools.ctl with K = 2 to 7 closes but allows a halt (6 to 429 abstract halting configurations).

claims.title: Defects drifting on a 100 background
claims.text: At the steps where E reaches a new cell on the right, written with ak = (100)^k: 10 a52 0 a22 10101010 a283 0 a358 1010 a102 0 (step 1,237,212), 10 a15 101010101010 a108 10101010 a1199 1110 a1 0 a954 1110 a747 1010 a3157 0 (step 59,431,697). The defects flip between forms such as 1010 and 1110 from one sample to the next, move left by about one block every few samples, and new ones appear at the right end; the leftmost one has moved from a64 to a15 between steps 2·105 and 6·107. Width 18,579 at step 59,431,697 (about 0.17·w2 steps).

claims.title: Does it halt?
claims.text: Not known. What is left is how the defects behave when they meet each other or the left end, and whether any meeting puts A on 11 or C on 01.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. Started on a blank tape, this Turing machine has run for 10<sup>9</sup> steps without stopping. This page runs the real machine in your browser, shows the shape of its run, and lists what is known, each result marked by what it rests on.

facts.text: No halt in the C simulator; 67,084 cells visited.
No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.
The growth shape of the two sides of the tape (see below).

sections.heading: A 100 background with defects
html: Writing ak for (100)^k, at the steps where E reaches a new cell on the right the tape reads:

Each right sweep shifts the background by one cell (A turns 100 into 001, D turns 001 into 010), and each defect alternates between two or three forms. The defects drift left at different speeds and new ones are born at the right end, so the gaps between them change slowly.

sections.heading: A on 11, or C on 01
html: The only halt is D reading a 1. D comes only from A reading a 1 (it writes 0 and moves right) or from C reading a 0 (it writes 1 and moves right), so the machine halts exactly when A meets 11 or C meets 01. Defects such as 1110 contain 11; the sweeps reach them in a phase where this does not happen. Whether a collision of defects, or a defect reaching the left end, can change that is the open question.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.054). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.483).
After 109 steps the tape spans 67,084 cells (65 left of the start, 53,425 right), with a density of 1s of 0.333.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: Related machines
html: Other holdouts of the list of 608 that are tied to this one. The comparison of tables is exact; everything about runs was checked on the first 107 steps of each machine and is an observation, not a proof (holdouts/related.py, holdouts/related.json).

Same table as the machines below, started in another state. Renaming the states as shown turns this machine's table into the other one, the halting transition included. The other machine starts in its own state A, which is not this machine's A: its run from blank tape is the run of this table started in another state. These are different runs: in the first 107 steps of each, no configuration of this machine's run occurs in any of the others, even up to a shift of the tape. So each of these holdouts is its own halting question, and settling one does not settle another.

summary: A bouncer over a background of (100)^n that carries small defects (1010, 1110, 10101010, ...): each sweep shifts the background and flips the defects between two phases, new defects are born at the right end and drift left at different speeds; it halts if A ever lands on 11 or C on 01.
